title: Is the Universe Actually Lopsided?
hook: Cosmology's standard model assumes the universe looks the same in every direction on the largest scales. A contested analysis argues the distribution of distant galaxies quietly fails that test.
key_points: The cosmic microwave background shows one side of the sky about one part in a thousand hotter than the other — a well-established 'CMB dipole.'
Standard cosmology predicts that the distribution of distant galaxies and quasars should show a matching dipole, for the same underlying reason.
A team led by Subir Sarkar (Oxford) argues that when tested (the Ellis-Baldwin test) on distant radio galaxies and quasars, the two dipoles don't line up.
If confirmed, this would undercut the assumption that the universe is isotropic on large scales — a foundation of the standard ΛCDM model — though the claim remains debated.
content_html: Modern cosmology rests on the assumption that, averaged over large enough scales, the universe looks roughly the same in every direction — no special axis, no lopsidedness. One famous piece of evidence for a "grain" in that smoothness is the cosmic microwave background's dipole: one side of the sky's afterglow radiation reads about one part in a thousand hotter than the other, usually explained as our own galaxy's motion relative to the early universe.
extra_html: If that explanation is right, the distribution of very distant galaxies and quasars should show a matching dipole pointing the same way, since it stems from the same underlying motion. A team led by Subir Sarkar (emeritus, University of Oxford), with Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, and Roya Mohayaee, applied the classic Ellis-Baldwin test to catalogs of distant radio galaxies and quasars — drawing on both ground-based radio telescopes and satellite mid-infrared surveys — and reports that the two dipoles don't line up as expected. The group argues this failure is arguably a more fundamental problem than the well-known Hubble tension, since it strikes at the assumption of cosmic isotropy itself rather than just a disputed expansion rate. If the mismatch holds up, it would force a rethink of the standard ΛCDM model's underlying geometry; for now, the result is real published research — in Reviews of Modern Physics — but remains a contested minority position within cosmology, not an accepted revision of the standard model.

related.title: The Hubble Tension: Cosmology's Stubborn Crisis
related.hook: Two trustworthy ways of measuring how fast the universe expands keep disagreeing — and a decade of cross-checks has only hardened the gap into a genuine crisis.

related.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
related.hook: The oldest light we can see is a faint glow filling all of space — released when the infant universe first cooled enough to become transparent, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

related.title: The Expanding Universe
related.hook: Distant galaxies are rushing away from us, and the farther one is, the faster it flees — not because they're moving through space, but because space itself is stretching.

related.title: Why Does Webb Keep Finding Things That Shouldn't Exist?
related.hook: JWST keeps spotting early black holes and galaxies that are too big, too bright, or too early to fit standard models — and cosmologists are racing to figure out which of many new theories is right.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'CMB dipole,' and how big is it?
flashcards.back_html: A pattern in the cosmic microwave background where one side of the sky is roughly one part in a thousand hotter than the opposite side.

flashcards.prompt: What test did Sarkar's team use to check whether distant galaxies show a matching dipole?

choices.text: The Ellis-Baldwin test, applied to distant radio galaxies and quasars
Direct imaging of the cosmic microwave background alone
Measuring the redshift of a single nearby galaxy

flashcards.explanation_html: The Ellis-Baldwin test compares how matter (galaxies, quasars) is distributed across the sky against the CMB's own dipole pattern, using independent radio and infrared surveys.

flashcards.prompt: What would it mean for cosmology if the two dipoles genuinely don't match — and how solid is that claim?
flashcards.back_html: It would challenge the assumption that the universe is isotropic (the same in every direction) on the largest scales — a pillar of the standard ΛCDM model. The claim is real research but remains debated, not settled consensus.
